messages.subject: meta analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm trying to conduct a fixed-effect meta-analysis using Genomic SEM. Before using sumstats function, I wanted to fit a base model as advised to see if the model fits well. I specified the model as below:

commonfactor.model <- 'F1 =~ 1*Pheno1 + 1*Pheno2
F1~~1*F1
Pheno1 ~~ 0* Pheno1
Pheno2 ~~ 0* Pheno2'

The model did not converge and I got the following error:

Error: The primary model did not converge! Additional warnings or errors are likely being printed by lavaan. The model output is also printed below (without standard errors) in case this is helpful for troubleshooting. Please note that these results should not be interpreted.

Would anyone be able to help?

Thank you very much in advance!
Alice

messages.subject: Re: Using genomic SEM in ecology: advice on minimum required sample sizes
messages.subject_clean: Using genomic SEM in ecology: advice on minimum required sample sizes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rebecca,

Because Genomic SEM relies heavily on the implementation of LDSC, (at least for human data) the minimum sample size is likely around 5000 effective sample sizes <https://github.com/bulik/ldsc/wiki/FAQ#genetic-correlation-and-heritability>. Neale lab also found that for UK Biobank data ~4500 effective sample size was required for "80% power to detect h2 ≥ 0.2 at nominal significance (p<.05)" <https://nealelab.github.io/UKBB_ldsc/confidence.html#minimum_sample_size>. You might be able to get better precision with lower sample size using HDL as noted here <https://rpubs.com/MichelNivard/640145>, but again this is all on European human data and it would require you to generate a separate reference panel.

Is there a way to calculate the heritability Z-score for your data? h2 Z > 4 is recommended for Genomic SEM I think.

Jeff

On Thursday, January 12, 2023 at 5:17:31 AM UTC-5 rsch...@gmail.com wrote:
> Dear group,
>
> I was hoping someone could advice me on the possibilities to use genomic SEM beyond human disease and crop breeding. Specifically, I am wondering what minimum sample sizes are recommended to run genomic SEM with adequate power.
>
> The studies I have found to date that use genomic SEM all have the privilege of working with human or plant data that contain over thousands of samples. However, these sample sizes are less common within ecology, although this approach would be of great use to identify genetically correlating traits in our field too. Therefore, I was wondering if there are any rules-of-thumb for conducting genomic SEM with regards to sample size and maximum number of traits one could test with it. Is it of any use to use this approach with sample sizes lower than 1,000?
>
> Many thanks,
> Rebecca

messages.subject: Re: Mediation effect estimated by GWAS by subtraction
messages.subject_clean: Mediation effect estimated by GWAS by subtraction
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

sure you could specifgy the following mediation model:

EA ~ b*Cog + direct*SNP
Cog ~ a*SNP
 mediated := a*b

total := mediated + direct

I want to emphasises that this mediation model is empirically misspecified as their is rather convincing evidence education causes Cog as well see:
Ritchie, S. J., & Tucker-Drob, E. M. (2018). How much does education improve intelligence? A meta-analysis. Psychological science, 29(8), 1358-1369.

This means that the estimates you'll get wont corresponds to any true effect.

You could, and this is something we got into in the supplements of the Cog/NonCog paper, specify this model:

EA ~ b*Cog + direct*SNP
Cog ~ 0.2*EA
Cog ~ a*SNP
 mediated := a*b

where you's have to get that fixed 0.2 (which is a random example don't just copy it!) form the literature, form that paper i references for example. Ideally you'd try a range of plausible values.

This model then still omits the  (plausible) effect of s SNP acting on BOTH Cog and NonCog trough a confounder.

At the end of the day these models are versions of the Cog/NonCog model reorganised the emphasise a different causal configuration, there are 2 traits and 1 SNP, you estimate the maximum allowable number of effects so the models are often  interchangeable.

messages.subject: HDL - NA in covariance
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am running into an issue where a certain trait produces NAs in the sampling covariance ($V) matrix in High Definition Likelihood.

I am essentially trying to replicate the GUT factor from this preprint <https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2022.10.03.510292v1.full>, but the primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) trait causes the entire sampling covariance matrix to turn into NaNs. There is some missingness (~2.5%) but other two traits Crohn's Disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC) have close to 3.5% missingness and still work fine on their own or with other traits. And from what I understand, HDL is robust to missingness and produces more conservative heritability estimates as missingness grows (up to 5% by author's testing).

I also noticed that on the covariance matrix ($S) PSC has 0 on the diagonal. Does that have something to do with the issue? Unfortunately HDL doesn't seem to have logs or error messages.

Regards,

Jeff

On Thursday, May 12, 2022 at 8:29:00 AM UTC+1 Matthijs van der Zee wrote:
> Hi  Kätlin,
>
> Lowering the number of cores in userGWAS will definitely save quite a bit of memory (as will setting the correct exports btw), as each core spawns a new R process with its own memory overhead, input data, etc. I tested this once albeit on a much smaller dataset and on windows (See v0.0.5 in PATCHNOTES.md on github), and memory usage of 12 cores was roughly 4x that of 1 core, though I should point out I expect the scaling to be less severe on Windows. So all in all, yes, lowering the cores will lower memory usage.
>
> However, lowering these significantly will lead to much slower runtimes than your machine is capable of which would be unfortunate, and I can't guarantee that it will be sufficient to solve all memory problems. What I would recommend you do is splitting your input data and running those separately, as follows:
> Rscript1: Runs everything up to your call to userGWAS, then saves a number of files with what will be the input of SNPs split into, let's say 5 parts with ~2M SNPs each. This should also save covstruc and everything else you provide as input to userGWAS.
> Rscript2: Runs userGWAS for a specific part (for how to provide arguments to an R script see https://www.r-bloggers.com/2015/09/passing-arguments-to-an-r-script-from-command-lines/) with input generated in Rscript1, saves the result of that part
> Rscript3: Merges all X (5 in my example) parts of Rscript2, how to do this will depend on the model and sub argument, but likely boils down to rbinding the individual elements of the resulting list. Everything else you want to do after userGWAS also goes here.
>
> This will of course still be slower than doing it all in 1 go, but I expect the runtime difference to be much smaller compared to a run with cores=4 instead of cores=15.
> All that being said,  this is more work than just lowering cores... So if runtime is not an issue at all, lowering the cores argument would be the easiest way.
>
> Let me know if that helps!
>
> Best,
> Matthijs
>
> Op donderdag 12 mei 2022 om 08:35:53 UTC+2 schreef katli...@gmail.com:
> > Hello,
> >
> > I am trying to run GWAS-by-subtraction in GenomicSEM and I am having out-of-memory issues. I am following the steps and models that are described in this tutorial: https://rpubs.com/MichelNivard/565885. The input is having more than 10 million SNPs. When running the analysis for top 1 million, the process completed successfully.
> > When running with 10M SNPs the userGWAS function consumes all the free memory (which is around 26GB) and then R gets killed. I am running this function using parallel=TRUE on a Linux machine with 8 cores and 16 threads. I have set the correct environment variables before starting R (export OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 NUMEXPR_NUM_THREADS=1 VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS=1).
> > I have also tried to reduce the amount of cores allocated for the function and this results in less memory being used initially but I am not sure if it actually postpones the process being killed or it can really help in avoiding the out-of-memory issues.
> >
> > Do you have any ideas how to solve this issue, can decreasing the amount of cores actually result in a smaller memory usage or it will only result in memory being used up more slowly but initially still in the same amount? Are there any other tips or tricks to try to get this function running?
> >
> > Thank you for your help!
> > Kätlin

Hi Alice,

The link below contains scripts to run a model in parallel on a computing cluster along with a word document that walks through them. These scripts use the userGWAS functions so you would want to swap that piece out, and the commands to request resources on your cluster in the 3b script will definitely need to be changed.

As I write in the top of the word document, errors that you get with these scripts can be due to cluster-specific ways that resources are requested, R is loaded, etc. that I won't know how to troubleshoot assuming I've never worked on your particular cluster. So these scripts will likely only serve as a starting point, and I would recommend talking to the cluster specific IT folks at your institution to get further help if needed. Hope this still helps!

Best,

messages.subject: Re: N specification in running sumstats
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,

Good question! Either should work. If you write N = NULL then the package will make a vector of NAs based on the number of files you feed it, so the end result is the same as providing a vector of NAs. Bottom line: N = NULL is probably the most straightforward.

The different specifications have to do with how the partially standardized beta (a GWAS beta standardized with respect to the variance in the phenotype but not the predictor [the genotype] is backed out from the data. If you are working with, for example, Z-stats only for a binary outcome vs. logistic betas vs. OLS betas then the way that partially standardized beta is backed out is going to differ. The logic for this is described in the method section of the original 2019 Genomic SEM paper.

Best,
  Andrew

messages.subject: Re: meta analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alice,

I don't think model fit is overly meaningful here since you are forcing the variables to have all of their variance accounted for by the latent factor (i.e., you aren't really theoretically interested in the factor itself, but really are just estimating a factor to do a meta-analysis). With that said there are two things I would point out:

1. The fit of the model you ran using unit loading identification and this model below using unit variance identification should fit the same (I just confirmed they do with a couple test cases). If they don't it could indicate more general problems with the output from LDSC.
commonfactor.model2 <- 'F1 =~ a*Pheno1 + a*Pheno2

Pheno1 ~~ 0* Pheno1
Pheno2 ~~ 0* Pheno2'

usermodel(covstruc,model=commonfactor.model2,std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE)

2. In the test cases I ran the model fit unsurprisingly continued to improve the more genetically correlated the variables were. While again I don't think model fit is all that useful here, I would argue that this might be signaling that you are trying to meta-analyze two variables that are not very correlated. If that's true, meta-analysis may not make the most sense here.

Best,
  Andrew
